title: U prodavnici
reviewerNotes: Full draft to Lesson 1 exemplar bar. ready for human review before publish.
storyBeat: Ana shops with Emir and practices želim, molim, hvala, and prices.

vocabulary: Name prodavnica, pijaca, kesa, and novac
Buy jabuka, banana, voda, and mlijeko
Ask Koliko košta and react with jeftino or skupo
grammar: Use Želim plus an object as one ready chunk
Keep molim and hvala in the polite kit
Reuse familiar present-tense frames from earlier lessons.
culture: Feel market energy in Tuzla, north of Sarajevo’s old bazaar
Use short polite routines to keep the queue moving

grammar.title: Želim + object
grammar.explanation: Learn this as a phrase, not a table. Želim means I want. Use it at the counter. Say Želim jabuku. Say Želim hljeb. Say Želim vodu. Feminine -a nouns often take -u in this chunk. Keep the list short and sayable.

grammar.title: Molim and hvala
grammar.explanation: Learn this as a phrase, not a table. Molim softens a request (Hljeb, molim.) and can also answer thank you as you’re welcome. Hvala is thank you. Stack them as Hvala! and Molim!

grammar.title: Koliko košta?
grammar.explanation: Learn this as a phrase, not a table. Ask the price with Koliko košta? Answer with a number and KM if you know it, or just react. Say To je jeftino. Say To je skupo.

culture.title: Market day energy in Tuzla
culture.body: Emir takes Ana shopping with photos from Tuzla in the northeast. One photo shows an old-town street. Another shows a public fountain. People there buy fruit by the kilogram like it is the most normal errand in the world. A prodavnica can be a tiny corner shop. A pijaca is the open market where voices, scales, and kesa bags do most of the work. Today’s language stays short on purpose. You say what you want, you ask the price, and you finish with hvala.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A: Shop words that move
lessonBlocks.body: Learn the places first. Prodavnica is a shop. Pijaca is a market. Add kesa for a bag and novac for money. Then stock the basket with jabuka, banana, voda, and mlijeko, plus hljeb from the last lesson. Practice pointing and naming before you speak full sentences. Emir makes Ana say mlijeko with lj, not a soft English milk guess.
tips: Prodavnica is a shop. Pijaca is a market.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B: Želim, molim, hvala
lessonBlocks.body: Run the counter script as full sentences. Say Želim jabuku, molim. Ask Koliko košta? Finish with Hvala! Grab a kesa. Decide whether the price is jeftino or skupo. Ana almost pays with the wrong coins, Emir laughs, and Mrvica somehow appears near the fruit crate as if she has a loyalty card.
tips: Keep Želim, molim, Koliko košta, and Hvala ready
React with jeftino or skupo after the price

conversation.setting: Amira sends Ana and Emir for fruit and milk. A shopkeeper weighs apples at a small counter.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.english: Two apples. How much does it cost?

practice.prompt: Write I want an apple (object form).
Write How much does it cost?
Write the Bosnian spelling for milk.

funFacts.title: KM on the price tag
funFacts.body: Shop prices in Bosnia and Herzegovina are written in convertible marks, or KM. You do not need a finance lecture to use the currency in a market line. Ask Koliko košta, hear a number, and pay. For this lesson, KM is simply the money word that makes shopping phrases real.

funFacts.title: Tuzla’s other fame
funFacts.body: Tuzla is a major northeast city with its own market rhythm. It is known for salt heritage and for a large urban center that is not Baščaršija. A shopping day there feels local and practical rather than tourist-postcard. That is why Emir uses Tuzla photos when Ana practices prodavnica language.

funFacts.title: Molim does double duty
funFacts.body: Molim is one of the most useful shop words in Bosnian. It can soften a request as please, and it can answer hvala as you’re welcome. Context tells you which meaning you just heard. Learn both uses now, because you will meet them in every polite purchase.

funFacts.title: Kesa is not optional
funFacts.body: Asking for a kesa is a normal end to a purchase. Fruit, bread, and bottles are easier to carry in a bag, and clerks expect the request. Saying Kesa, molim also gives you one more clean practice of molim. Leave the counter with the bag and the phrase both under control.

civicContext.title: Tuzla’s factories closed faster than new jobs arrived
civicContext.body: Tuzla’s postwar story is one of industrial jobs disappearing faster than steady replacements arrived. The city was a major mining, chemical, and energy center that employed large parts of the region. After the war, many plants shrank or closed through damage, privatization, and market collapse, leaving long stretches of unemployment and insecure work. Markets and small shops kept daily shopping alive, but they did not replace the industrial wages that once supported whole neighborhoods.
